  [2] File: scripts/review_issue_ledger.sh (line ~202)
      Problem: The `flush_block` function in the `parse_review_issues` awk script prints the `code` variable directly into a TSV field without escaping newlines. The `current_code` variable can contain newlines (as built up in the collect_code logic at lines 278-283 where it does `current_code = current_code "\n" t`). When multi-line code is present, the resulting TSV record spans multiple physical lines.; The downstream awk script (line 640) reads the TSV with `awk -F '\t'` expecting single-line records. When CURRENT_CODE contains newlines (common for multi-line code snippets in review findings), the TSV format is corrupted. This causes field misalignment when the second awk script or the bash read loop (line 733 with `while IFS=$'\t' read -r block_id...`) consumes the file. The `current_code` field (position $7 in parsed_current_file, position $8 in current_with_ids_file) would be truncated at the first newline, causing incorrect hash computation, wrong lifecycle transitions (NEW/PERSISTING/FIXED/RESURGENT), and potentially dropped or duplicated issues.; The tests pass only because all test fixtures use single-line CURRENT_CODE values. According to docs/review-pipeline-improvements.md, CURRENT_CODE is explicitly a multi-line field for multi-line code findings.; **ISSUE 2: Missing SUPPORT_SCRIPTS_DIR definition**

While AWK internal variables handle this, the resulting `out_file` contains record separators (newlines) in the middle of a logical record's data.; Subsequent consumers of this TSV file (the floor-tagging AWK and the bash `while read` loop) read the file line-by-line using `\n` as a record separator.   [10] File: scripts/review_issue_ledger.sh
      Problem: The script uses `git cat-file -e "HEAD:${file_path}"` to verify file existence for anchor context extraction.; In "Implement" tasks or PRs adding new files, a file may exist in the working tree but not yet in `HEAD`. The script will fail the git check and falls back to `sed` on the local file. If the file is not yet committed AND `sed` fails (or if the file is only in the git index but not on disk), it returns an empty string. This causes all issues in new files to suffer from "anchor collision," where different issues in the same file get the same ID because their anchor context is identical (empty).
      Confidence: avg 4.0
